traveler: Alexandra David-Néel (Louise Eugénie Alexandrine Marie David; Alexandra Myrial; Yeshe Tome)
title: Beyond the Garden Gate: the Opera Singer Who Walked Into Lhasa
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Saint-Mandé, the birth outside the gate of Paris
stops.date_confidence: attested; EN and FR Wikipedia agree on date and commune
stops.campa: In Saint-Mandé, a mile beyond the eastern gate of Paris, Louise Eugénie Alexandrine Marie David is born to a Huguenot schoolmaster active in republican and anarchist circles and to a Belgian Catholic mother. The father has known the Commune's men; the mother keeps the Church. The child is given four names and will use none of them, signing herself first Alexandra Myrial on opera bills and then Alexandra David-Néel on the title pages of thirty books. She is born in the year Helena Blavatsky later told her followers she was living at Shigatse, under the Panchen Lama's roof.
suggested_refs: The birth register of Saint-Mandé, Seine, October 1868
sources: Foster & Foster, The Secret Lives of Alexandra David-Néel (1998)

stops.name: Père-Lachaise, the wall of the Communards
stops.date_confidence: biographers' tradition; the year is the year of the Commune, the day is not recorded
stops.campa: Her father walks the small child up the cemetery hill to the wall where the last Communards were shot. He shows her the brickwork. Biographers date her politics to this walk: at thirty she will publish Pour la vie, an individualist tract, and compose a treatise on the rights of women that Élisée Reclus, the anarchist geographer, agrees to preface and that goes into five languages. The gate of the garden and the wall of the executed stand at the two ends of one childhood, and she leaves by way of the gate.
suggested_refs: The Mur des Fédérés at Père-Lachaise, Paris
sources: Foster & Foster, The Secret Lives of Alexandra David-Néel

stops.name: Ixelles, Brussels, the family crosses the border
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1873-1874; FR Wikipedia gives the move and the district, not a month
stops.campa: The Davids leave France for Belgium and settle at Ixelles in Brussels, where Alexandra is schooled. Her formal education happens in a country not her own, and so will every education she gets afterward. She reads Jules Verne and she reads the Theosophists. In the Brussels house she sits at one table as a Catholic mother's daughter and a republican father's daughter. She settles that the way she will settle most things later: she goes out of the door and stays out until the question has stopped mattering.
suggested_refs: The David household at Ixelles, Brussels, 1870s

stops.name: Vlissingen, the first bolt
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1883 (age fifteen); no month given. The bicycle in some accounts belongs to a later escapade into Spain and is struck here
stops.campa: At fifteen, on a family holiday at Ostend, she absconds north up the coast for the Dutch port of Flessingue, meaning to take a boat for England. She has not the money for the passage and turns back. It is the first of several bolts: she will later ride alone into Spain, and at forty-two she will tell her husband she expects to be away nineteen months and stay fourteen years. What limits her is never permission and never nerve. It is fare, and she spends the next twenty years earning it.
suggested_refs: The Ostend to Flushing coast road, taken alone in 1883
sources: Foster & Foster, The Secret Lives of Alexandra David-Néel

stops.name: London, the British Museum and Madame Blavatsky's circle
stops.date_confidence: reading room and Theosophical circle attested to 1889; the earlier study 'at Madame Blavatsky's Theosophical Society' is dated only by her age, c. 1886-1888, and the pool's 'Paris' is unsupported since Blavatsky was at Ostend in 1886 and reached London only in May 1887
stops.campa: She reads in the library of the British Museum and moves in the Theosophical circles Helena Blavatsky has drawn around herself in London. At eighteen she had studied at Blavatsky's society; the older woman is living at Ostend in 1886 and reaches London only in May 1887, so the years overlap the Belgian coast of her own girlhood. In 1889 she takes Buddhism for her own and keeps the diary she will publish as La Lampe de sagesse. No teacher receives her into it and no rite marks the day. She decides it by herself, in a reading room, and treats the question as closed for the next eighty years.
stops.quote: When I adopted the principles of Buddhism, I knew not a single Buddhist, and was perhaps the only Buddhist in Paris.
stops.quote_source: David-Néel, quoted in David Guy, 'Alexandra David-Neel,' Tricycle: The Buddhist Review (1995)
suggested_refs: The British Museum reading room; La Lampe de sagesse (1896), her conversion diary
sources: Foster & Foster, The Secret Lives of Alexandra David-Néel

stops.name: Adyar, the Theosophical Society headquarters
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1891 by Foster & Foster; no month recorded
stops.campa: A small inheritance buys her a passage to India, and she goes first to Adyar outside Madras, to the compound Blavatsky and Olcott raised as the world headquarters of the Theosophical Society. Its library is the West's clearing house for Hindu and Buddhist texts, and its verandas are where Europeans going east are told what to look for. She is twenty-two and unaccompanied, and she is spending her legacy on a journey rather than on a settlement. The money runs out. She goes home and sings for a living.
suggested_refs: The Adyar library and headquarters compound of the Theosophical Society, Madras
sources: Foster & Foster, The Secret Lives of Alexandra David-Néel

stops.name: Varanasi, the ascetic on the river
stops.date_confidence: meeting attested to the 1891 visit; the month is inferred and the exact site within the city is not fixed across sources, so the ghat pin is approximate
stops.campa: On the river at Benares she seeks out Swami Bhaskarananda Saraswati, an ascetic who receives visitors in a garden and wears nothing at all, and studies with him briefly. She will call the encounter formative for the next sixty years. Sources do not agree on where in the city it happened. She is twenty-two, and the inheritance that paid for the passage is nearly gone. Eighty-two years after this, her secretary will carry her ashes and Yongden's down these same ghats and pour them into this water together.
suggested_refs: The ghats of Varanasi; the garden hermitage of Swami Bhaskarananda Saraswati
sources: David-Néel journals cited in Foster & Foster

stops.name: Hanoi, first soprano at the opera
stops.date_confidence: engagement attested to 1895-1897; the pin marks the Hanoi opera house site, though the present building was raised 1901-1911 and postdates her seasons
stops.campa: The inheritance gone, she takes the stage name Alexandra Myrial and sings first soprano in French Indochina: Violetta in La traviata, Marguerite in Faust, before the administrators and their wives. A Buddhist convert and an anarchist pamphleteer is earning her living in a colonial theatre singing French roles to colonial officials. She keeps the two lives from touching. The audiences do not know, the company does not know, and the husband she has not yet met will spend forty years finding out.
suggested_refs: Opera-Comique touring company programmes for Indochina, 1895-1897
sources: Foster & Foster, The Secret Lives of Alexandra David-Néel

stops.name: Montmartre, the anarchist pen
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Pour la vie (1898) and the 1899 treatise are attested; no Paris address for their composition is documented, so the quarter is a placement and not a record
stops.campa: Between engagements she writes for the French periodicals in the individualist register her father's house taught her. Pour la vie appears in 1898; the next year a treatise on the rights of women carries a preface by Élisée Reclus and is translated into five languages. No address is documented for any of it. The woman who will be received in audience by the thirteenth Dalai Lama and by the Panchen Lama at Tashilhunpo begins in print as an enemy of established authority of every kind, including the kind that will receive her.
suggested_refs: Pour la vie (1898); the 1899 treatise on women's rights, prefaced by Élisée Reclus
sources: Foster & Foster, The Secret Lives of Alexandra David-Néel

stops.name: Tunis, the engineer and the marriage
stops.date_confidence: marriage date attested; the July 1900 meeting at the Théâtre municipal and the 1902 casino directorship are attested separately and folded into this stop
stops.campa: Singing in Tunis in July 1900, after a season in Athens, she meets Philippe Néel de Saint-Sauveur, her distant cousin and chief engineer of the Tunisian railways. The courtship runs four years and mostly by letter. She leaves the stage in 1902 and spends a season directing the Tunis casino, and on the fourth of August 1904 they marry. The marriage lasts thirty-seven years and is conducted almost entirely on paper. From 1911 he pays for her journeys and reads about them by post.
suggested_refs: The Théâtre municipal de Tunis; the David-Néel correspondence, thirty-seven years of letters
sources: Foster & Foster, The Secret Lives of Alexandra David-Néel

stops.name: Paris, departure for nineteen months
stops.date_confidence: departure date attested; the port of embarkation is not named in any source consulted, so the pin is the Paris node and not a quay
stops.campa: On the ninth of August 1911 she leaves for Asia a third time, forty-two years old, funded by her husband and carrying a commission to study Buddhism where it is practised. She tells Philippe she expects to be gone about nineteen months. She lands back in France in May 1925. In the fourteen years between, she will live in a Himalayan cave, be expelled from India by the British Empire, cross the Gobi with a caravan, and walk into Lhasa in soot and yak hair beside a monk she has not yet met.
suggested_refs: The 1911 letters to Philippe Néel setting the length of the journey

stops.name: Kalimpong, audience with the thirteenth Dalai Lama
stops.date_confidence: date attested; place contested, a minority of sources put the audience at Darjeeling rather than at Bhutan House, Kalimpong. Pin inherited from the atlas Kalimpong node
stops.campa: At Bhutan House in Kalimpong, where the thirteenth Dalai Lama is waiting out his exile from a Lhasa held by Chinese troops, she is received in audience on the fifteenth of April 1912. He blesses her study and undertakes to answer her doctrinal questions in writing. A minority of sources place the meeting at Darjeeling instead. Forty-three years later Helena Roerich will die in this same hill town, and four years after that the fourteenth Dalai Lama will come out over the passes above it into the same exile.
suggested_refs: Bhutan House, Kalimpong, residence of the exiled thirteenth Dalai Lama

stops.name: Lachen, the hermit above the village
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1912; the cave residence runs intermittently to 1916 and the altitude of roughly four thousand metres is the figure given in the biographies
stops.campa: North up the Teesta at Lachen she meets the Gomchen of Lachen, a hermit who has spent years walled into retreat, and becomes his pupil. He gives her the religious name Yeshe Tome, Lamp of Wisdom. She settles in a cave hermitage at some four thousand metres above the village and spends much of the next four years there, learning Tibetan and the practice of tummo, the generated heat. A French opera singer of forty-three keeps a Himalayan winter in a hole in a cliff, and does not come down.
stops.quote: You have seen the ultimate and supreme light. It isn't in a year or two of meditation that one arrives at the concepts you express.
stops.quote_source: The Gomchen of Lachen to David-Néel, quoted in David Guy, 'Alexandra David-Neel,' Tricycle: The Buddhist Review (1995)
suggested_refs: The hermitage above Lachen, Sikkim, occupied 1914-1916

stops.name: Darjeeling, the gate everyone uses
stops.date_confidence: no single dated David-Néel event anchors this stop; the year is a placement within her Sikkim residence and the pin is the atlas Darjeeling node, held for the corridor rather than for an incident
stops.campa: Darjeeling and Kalimpong are where the Tibetan frontier is stocked: porters hired, permits refused, expeditions weighed and assembled. Blavatsky was turned back at this frontier by the British in 1856. Hermann Keyserling climbed above the town in March 1912 to watch dawn come onto Kanchenjunga. In December 1923 Nicholas Roerich takes Talai Pho-Brang, the villa the exiled Dalai Lama had used, and stages five years of expedition out of it. Giuseppe Tucci will assemble eight expeditions from these streets between 1930 and 1948.
suggested_refs: The Darjeeling and Kalimpong outfitting trade, 1850-1950

stops.name: Gangtok, the crown prince and the boy
stops.date_confidence: Sidkeong Tulku's sudden death is attested to December 1914. The meeting with Yongden is attested to 1914 at a Sikkim monastery, aged fifteen; one entry in the research pool dated it October 1912 near Darjeeling and is contradicted by both language editions
stops.campa: She moves in and out of Gangtok, close to the Sikkimese royal house and above all to the crown prince Sidkeong Tulku, a reforming monk-prince who dies suddenly in December 1914. In one of these Sikkim monasteries in the same year she meets Aphur Yongden, fifteen years old, and takes him into her service. He will guide her, translate for her, walk to Lhasa at her side, be adopted as her son in 1929, and die in her house in Provence forty-one years afterward. The prince dies. The boy stays.
suggested_refs: The Sikkimese royal house at Gangtok under Sidkeong Tulku, died December 1914

stops.name: Tashilhunpo, Shigatse, received by the Panchen Lama
stops.date_confidence: attested. The lama is the ninth Panchen Lama, Thubten Choekyi Nyima; one entry in the research pool called him the sixth, who died in 1780. Pin inherited from the atlas Shigatse node
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of July 1916 she crosses into Tibet without permission, with Yongden and a monk, against the British edict that closes the country. Six days later she is at Tashilhunpo outside Shigatse and is received by the ninth Panchen Lama, who grants her honorary titles and the run of his libraries and lets her study texts closed to almost every other foreigner who has asked. Unlike travelers whose claims to this same shrine rest on word alone, David-Néel arrives here with a verified date attached to it.
suggested_refs: Tashilhunpo Monastery, seat of the Panchen Lamas; the honorary titles granted July 1916
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Thubten Choekyi Nyima, 9th Panchen Lama'

stops.name: Peking, expelled into a continent
stops.date_confidence: the deportation notice is attested to 1916 without a month; the Japan, Korea and China passage to 1917-1918. Day and month here are placements
stops.campa: The British answer the unauthorized crossing with a deportation notice, and Sikkim, her base for four years, closes behind her. Europe is at war and there is no passage home. So she goes the other way: Japan, then Korea, then Peking, and from Peking westward across China with Yongden in a caravan, through the Gobi and over the Mongolian steppe, some thousands of miles overland toward the Tibetan marches. An expulsion from a hundred miles of frontier turns, in her hands, into the crossing of a continent.
suggested_refs: The British India deportation notice of 1916; the 1917-1918 caravan route across China and Mongolia

stops.name: Kumbum Monastery, three years of translation
stops.date_confidence: residence attested to 1918-1921; no month. Coordinate corrected to the surveyed position of Ta'er Si, Huangzhong, about two kilometres from the figure carried in the research pool
stops.campa: At Kumbum in Amdo, the birthplace of Tsongkhapa and one of the great Gelug seats, she and Yongden are given quarters and stay about three years. She works at the Prajnaparamita, the perfection-of-wisdom literature, translating with him at her elbow. It is the longest settled stretch of her Asian life. Six years later, walking into Lhasa in rags, she will be able to answer a monk's question in his own idiom and in the register a pilgrim would use, which no amount of soot on a face can do for her.
suggested_refs: Kumbum (Ta'er Si) Monastery, Qinghai; her partial translation of the Prajnaparamita

stops.name: Atuntze, Yunnan, provisioning the disguise
stops.date_confidence: the final approach is staged from the Yunnan-Tibet borderlands in 1923; the month is her own account's autumn departure and is not independently fixed
stops.campa: From the border country near Atuntze she and Yongden set out for Lhasa on foot with what the two of them can carry. She blackens her face with soot and Chinese ink, braids yak hair into her own, and travels as an arjopa, a poor pilgrim walking to the holy city. Yongden, an ordained lama who reads, travels as her son. Earlier attempts have been stopped at the frontier by British and Tibetan officials alike. This one carries no papers to be examined and no baggage train to be seen from a ridge.
stops.quote: I had chosen to travel as an arjopa because it is the best disguise to pass without attracting notice. Yongden, who is an authentic and well-read lama, looked his part perfectly, and I, his aged mother, who had undertaken a long pilgrimage for devotional reasons, constituted a rather touching and sympathetic figure.
stops.quote_source: My Journey to Lhasa (1927), ch. I
suggested_refs: My Journey to Lhasa (1927), the chapters on the disguise and its provisioning

stops.name: Markam, the country of the parallel rivers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and internally contradictory. The pool labels this a Salween crossing, but the coordinate sits at Markam in the Mekong corridor; at this latitude the Salween runs near 97 degrees east, about 150 km west. The pin is kept and the river name is left open
stops.campa: The route west runs through the gorge country where three of Asia's great rivers run parallel within a hundred miles of one another, the Salween, the Mekong and the Yangtze, each in a trench thousands of feet deep. They ford in winter. She kept the geography of this stretch deliberately vague in print, to protect the villagers who fed and hid them from official reprisal, so the reconstructions later biographers have drawn of her line of march disagree with each other, and with her, and with the map.
suggested_refs: The Three Parallel Rivers country of eastern Tibet and northwest Yunnan

stops.name: Dokar La, the pass in the snow
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No independently surveyed coordinate for a pass under the name she gives has been confirmed; the position is read off her narrative
stops.campa: Her own account describes a high pass she calls the Dokar La, crossed in freezing weather, the two of them sleeping in snow without a fire and living on dried barley flour. When a robber band or a suspicious headman appears on the road, Yongden speaks and she keeps her face down and her mouth shut, an old woman on pilgrimage who is not worth robbing. No pass under that name has been fixed on a modern map. What is attested is the book, and the book says they crossed it.
suggested_refs: My Journey to Lhasa (1927), the winter passes of the westward march

stops.name: Chaksam, the ferry over the Tsangpo
stops.date_confidence: attested crossing point; coordinate corrected to the historic Chaksam ferry by Qüxü (Chushul), about 24 km east of the figure carried in the research pool
stops.campa: The last obstacle is the Yarlung Tsangpo, crossed by the traditional ferry at Chaksam near Chushul, hide boats worked across the current on the route every pilgrim to Lhasa uses. Yongden tells her not to speak too soon: the river Kyi is still to come. On the far bank the road runs up the valley into the city, and the crowds thicken with pilgrims coming in for the Monlam prayer festival. That crowd is the cover she has been walking four months to reach, and it holds.
suggested_refs: The Chaksam ferry over the Yarlung Tsangpo at Qüxü

stops.name: Lhasa, the Potala sighted at dawn
stops.date_confidence: arrival attested to February 1924, during the Monlam festival crowds; no exact day. Pin inherited from the atlas Potala node
stops.campa: Coming up the valley they sight the Potala on its rock. Years earlier, at a frontier post where she had been turned back and marched away under escort, she swore that she would reach this city, and she has walked in beggar's rags to keep that vow. She is the first Western woman known to enter it. Other travelers' claims to this same city rest on word alone. Hers rests on a printed narrative, a date, and two months of streets that she can describe from memory.
stops.quote_source: My Journey to Lhasa (1927), ch. VII, on first sighting the Potala
suggested_refs: The Potala Palace, Lhasa; My Journey to Lhasa (1927), ch. VII

stops.name: Jokhang, inside the disguise
stops.date_confidence: the Jokhang visit is attested to the two months in the city; the day is a placement within February 1924
stops.campa: In the Jokhang, the oldest and holiest shrine in Tibet, she circles with the pilgrims and prostrates with them, a beggar-woman from a far province whose odd accent is explained by distance. Nobody stops her. She stays about two months in the city, walking the streets and pricing the markets and committing both to memory, with a compass and a revolver under the rags and no permission of any kind from the government whose capital she is quietly measuring. The soot and the yak hair are doing the work a passport does.
stops.quote: Lha gyalo. De tamche pam! We are at Lhasa!
stops.quote_source: Aphur Yongden on entering the city, recorded in My Journey to Lhasa (1927), ch. VII
suggested_refs: The Jokhang temple, Lhasa, and the pilgrim circuit of the Barkhor

stops.name: Drepung, the three great seats
stops.date_confidence: the monastery visits are attested to the 1924 stay without individual dates; the month is a placement
stops.campa: She visits Drepung, at that date among the largest monastic communities on earth, and Sera on the northern edge of the city, and Ganden on its ridge above the Kyi: the three Gelug seats that make Lhasa a capital of the mind as well as a seat of government. She walks into them as a pilgrim, which is the only condition on which she could have walked into them at all. Twenty-four years later Giuseppe Tucci will arrive with permits, an escort and cameras, and be received at the Potala by a Dalai Lama of thirteen.
suggested_refs: Drepung, Sera and Ganden, the three Gelug seats of the Lhasa valley

stops.name: Samye, the oldest monastery
stops.date_confidence: French sources list Samye among the houses reached; day and month are placements. Pin inherited from the atlas Samye node, which sits west of the surveyed monastery at 29.3255, 91.5037; note also that Samye lies well southeast of the Lhasa valley, so 'circuit around Lhasa' is loose
stops.campa: Samye, founded in the eighth century by Padmasambhava and Shantarakshita and laid out as a model of the universe in stone, is the oldest monastery in Tibet, and it stands across the Tsangpo a long way southeast of the Lhasa valley. The French sources list it among the houses she reaches on this journey. Giuseppe Tucci will study its mandala plan on the central-Tibet expedition of 1937, the two of them working the same walls thirteen years apart and never once meeting on the page.
suggested_refs: Samye Monastery, its mandala plan and eighth-century foundation

stops.name: Lhasa, the Sertreng and the daily wash
stops.date_confidence: the Tsomchö Sertreng attendance on 4 April is attested; the denunciation to Tsarong Shapé is attested to the same stay without a date
stops.campa: On the fourth of April she stands in the crowd below the Potala for the Tsomchö Sertreng, the great annual display, still in her rags. What nearly ends the whole thing is hygiene. A beggar who goes down to the river to wash every day is a beggar who is not one, and she is denounced on that ground to the governor Tsarong Shapé. She leaves the city before the authorities move. Two months undetected in the forbidden capital, and the near miss comes from washing her face.
stops.quote: I was in Lhasa. No doubt I could be proud of my victory, but the struggle, with cunning and trickery as weapons, was not yet over.
stops.quote_source: My Journey to Lhasa (1927), ch. VII (one word restored from an OCR artifact in the 1927 scan)
suggested_refs: The Tsomchö Sertreng ceremony at the Potala, 4 April 1924

stops.name: Gyantse, the identity given up
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1924; the host is contested, and the coordinate is corrected to the surveyed Gyantse Dzong, 1.4 km north of the figure carried in the research pool
stops.campa: Leaving Lhasa she comes down to Gyantse under its dzong and gives herself up as what she is. The sources disagree about who took her in. The French say Frank Ludlow, head of the English school at Gyantse; the English credit David Macdonald, the British trade agent at Yatung, who certainly lent her five hundred rupees and arranged her papers with his son-in-law Captain Perry. Both accounts may be true, and neither is chosen over the other here. She leaves Tibet through the Chumbi valley in borrowed clothes.
suggested_refs: Gyantse Dzong; the British trade agency at Yatung in the Chumbi valley

stops.name: Calcutta, arranging the passage home
stops.date_confidence: the Calcutta stay is attested to 1924-1925 without months; the date here is a placement between Gyantse in May and Le Havre in May 1925
stops.campa: Down from the Chumbi valley she reaches Calcutta and books her return. The news has gone ahead of her: the papers already have the story of the Frenchwoman who walked into Lhasa. She is fifty-six, has not seen Europe in thirteen years, and is going home with notebooks, photographs, a Tibetan son who is not yet legally hers, and a manuscript that will make her famous within two years and be disputed for the rest of the century and past the end of it.
suggested_refs: The Calcutta press of 1924 on the first Western woman in Lhasa

stops.name: Le Havre, the boat comes in
stops.date_confidence: date given by both language editions; the pool tags the Le Havre landing itself as a reconstruction in one entry and as attested in another, and the discrepancy is not resolved
stops.campa: She lands at Le Havre on the tenth of May 1925 and Philippe Néel is on the quay. She had told him nineteen months. The press meets the boat. She settles for a few years at Toulon and writes the journey up, and Voyage d'une Parisienne à Lhassa comes out in 1927 in Paris, London and New York at once. The argument starts with it: the tummo heat, the runners who travel in trance, and whether a European woman of fifty-five had done the thing she says she did.
stops.quote: Before the frontier post to which I had been escorted I took an oath that in spite of all obstacles I would reach Lhasa and show what the will of a woman could achieve!
suggested_refs: Voyage d'une Parisienne à Lhassa (1927); My Journey to Lhasa, the simultaneous London and New York editions

stops.name: Digne-les-Bains, the fortress of meditation
stops.date_confidence: the house is bought in 1928 and enlarged from 1932; Mystiques et magiciens du Tibet and the legal adoption of Yongden both fall in 1929, without months
stops.campa: In 1928 she buys a small house at Digne in the Basses-Alpes, enlarges it from 1932, and names it Samten Dzong, fortress of meditation: the first Lamaist hermitage and shrine in France. Mystiques et magiciens du Tibet appears in 1929, and in the same year she legally adopts Aphur Yongden as her son. Out of this house will come more than thirty books, most of them about a country she is now barred from entering, written within sight of the Provençal hills by a woman who learned her Tibetan in a cave.
stops.quote: I shut myself in [retreat] and proceeded to perform the prescribed concentration of thought and other rites. After a few months the phantom monk was formed. His form grew gradually fixed and life-like looking. He became a kind of guest, living in my apartment.
stops.quote_source: Magic and Mystery in Tibet (1929/1931), ch. VIII, on the deliberate creation of a tulpa
suggested_refs: Samten Dzong, Digne-les-Bains; Mystiques et magiciens du Tibet (1929)
sources: David-Néel, Magic and Mystery in Tibet

stops.name: Moscow, the Trans-Siberian at sixty-nine
stops.date_confidence: the departure via Brussels and the Trans-Siberian is attested to 1937; no month is given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: At sixty-nine, with Europe visibly walking into another war, she goes again: Brussels, Moscow, and the Trans-Siberian eastward, meaning to study Taoism in China. She arrives into the second Sino-Japanese war instead. Yongden travels with her, thirty-eight years old, a Sikkimese monk taken back east by his adoptive French mother. She will not see France again for nine years, and by the time she does she will be a widow and the war she was avoiding will have been fought and finished behind her.
suggested_refs: The 1937 Trans-Siberian route from Brussels to Manchuria

stops.name: Wutai Shan, the mountain of Manjushri
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1937-1938; the month is a placement inside that window
stops.campa: She reaches Peking and goes on to Wutai Shan in Shanxi, the five-terraced mountain sacred to Manjushri, where Chinese and Tibetan Buddhism have shared the same slopes for a thousand years and Mongol pilgrims still come up in caravans. The Japanese army is moving through north China around her. She is sixty-nine years old on a pilgrimage mountain inside a war zone, taking notes, and when she moves she moves southwest toward the Tibetan marches rather than back toward any port.
suggested_refs: Wutai Shan, the shared Chinese and Tibetan pilgrimage mountain

stops.name: Tachienlu, five years on the old frontier
stops.date_confidence: the sources conflict on the day: English Wikipedia gives 4 June 1938, French gives 4 July 1938. The June date is carried here and the conflict is not resolved. She stays to 1944, passing through Chengdu on the way in
stops.campa: She settles at Tachienlu on the old Sino-Tibetan frontier, the town where Chinese Sichuan ends and Kham begins, and stays five years through the war, working with Yongden and writing Sous des nuées d'orage. Bombing, famine and banditry pass through the district around her. In 1941 a letter reaches her here with the news that Philippe Néel is dead. She had been married to him thirty-seven years and had been away from him for thirty of them. She goes on working.
suggested_refs: Sous des nuées d'orage, written at Tachienlu during the war years

stops.name: Calcutta, out by air
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1946; no day recorded
stops.campa: At seventy-seven she is flown out of Calcutta with Yongden, helped by the French consul Christian Fouchet. She had come east the first time by steamer in 1911 and had once gone west across China by caravan through the Gobi. She leaves the continent for the last time in an aeroplane, in a few hours, over the ground it took her years to walk. Thirty-five years after telling Philippe Néel nineteen months, she flies home to a house he paid for and never lived in.
suggested_refs: The 1946 evacuation flight from Calcutta arranged by consul Christian Fouchet

stops.name: Paris, the traveling ends
stops.date_confidence: arrival in Paris attested to 1 July 1946, return to Digne to October of the same year
stops.campa: She lands in Paris on the first of July 1946 and goes down to Digne in October. She is seventy-seven and the traveling is finished, though she will not concede that for another twenty-two years. What is left is the work: Textes tibétains inédits in 1952, carrying the erotic poems attributed to the sixth Dalai Lama, and a long shelf of translation and commentary produced in a Provençal house by a woman who learned her Tibetan from a hermit in Sikkim.
suggested_refs: Textes tibétains inédits (1952)

stops.name: Samten Dzong, Yongden dies
stops.date_confidence: date attested by both language editions. Her age at his death was 86, not 87: born 24 October 1868, she turned 87 seventeen days afterward, and the French article's arithmetic is wrong
stops.campa: Aphur Yongden dies suddenly of kidney failure at Samten Dzong on the seventh of October 1955, fifty-six years old. He had walked from Sikkim to Lhasa beside her, spoken for her at every checkpoint where her accent would have finished them, been her son in French law for twenty-six years, and had been expected by everyone, herself included, to outlive a woman thirty-one years his senior. She is eighty-six, seventeen days short of eighty-seven. She keeps his ashes in the house and does not bury them.
suggested_refs: The chapel at Samten Dzong, where Yongden's ashes waited eighteen years

stops.name: Monaco, walking on her arms
stops.date_confidence: the Monaco period is attested to April 1957; no day. The coordinate is a town-level pin, since the sources record hotels rather than an address
stops.campa: She leaves Digne and lives in Monaco for a period, moving from hotel to hotel, her rheumatism so far gone that she says she walks on her arms. One English source has her resident at Samten Dzong only from 1925 to 1957, which cannot be squared with her dying there in 1969, and no source describes the return; the gap stands here rather than being filled with an invented journey. She is in her ninetieth year, in a principality of casinos, having last kept a fixed address in the Himalaya.
suggested_refs: The Monaco hotel years, 1957 onward

stops.name: Digne-les-Bains, the secretary and the last books
stops.date_confidence: The Secret Oral Teachings is dated 1964, Immortalité et réincarnation to 1961, the Peyronnet engagement to June 1959; the stop is anchored on the 1964 book and no month is recorded
stops.campa: In June 1959 she engages Marie-Madeleine Peyronnet as her secretary, and Peyronnet stays to the end and becomes her heir. The books keep coming out of the house: Immortalité et réincarnation in 1961, and in 1964, with Yongden's name still on the title page nine years after his death, The Secret Oral Teachings in the Tibetan Buddhist Sects. She is in her ninety-sixth year and writing that most of those who call themselves Buddhists have built kinds of Buddhism which are anything but Buddhist.
stops.quote: the primary recommendation that the Masters give to neophytes is: "Doubt!" Doubt is an incitement to research, and research is the Way which leads to Knowledge.
stops.quote_source: The Secret Oral Teachings in the Tibetan Buddhist Sects (1964), with Lama Yongden, p.15
suggested_refs: The Secret Oral Teachings in the Tibetan Buddhist Sects (1964)
sources: David-Néel and Yongden, The Secret Oral Teachings (1964)

stops.name: Digne-les-Bains, the passport renewed
stops.date_confidence: May 1968 is given plainly by the French article and by two further entries in the research pool; a fourth entry dates it 1969 and hedges it as unverified tradition, and that entry is the outlier. The counter or office inside the prefecture is not documented
stops.campa: In May 1968, five months short of a hundred, she goes to the prefecture at Digne and renews her passport, telling those around her that she means to return to Tibet. She does not make the journey. The document is valid and the country it would have carried her into has been shut to foreigners since 1950, the year the Chinese army entered and the fieldwork of every European on the plateau ended at once. She is the last living person who walked into Lhasa without asking anyone.
suggested_refs: The prefecture of the Basses-Alpes at Digne; the 1968 passport

stops.name: Samten Dzong, the death at a hundred
stops.date_confidence: attested; both language editions agree on date and place
stops.campa: She dies at Samten Dzong on the eighth of September 1969, six weeks short of a hundred and one, in the house she named fortress of meditation, with Yongden's ashes in the chapel and Peyronnet in the next room. She was born in the year Blavatsky claimed to be living at Shigatse and she outlived the Tibet she walked into: the Chinese entered in 1950, the frontier closed behind Giuseppe Tucci and everyone else, and in 1959 the fourteenth Dalai Lama came out over the passes above Kalimpong.
stops.quote: Ever since I was five years old, a tiny precocious child of Paris, I wished to move out of the narrow limits in which, like all children of my age, I was then kept. I craved to go beyond the garden gate, to follow the road that passed it by, and to set out for the Unknown.
stops.quote_source: My Journey to Lhasa (1927), Introduction, p.16
suggested_refs: Samten Dzong, now the Fondation Alexandra David-Néel museum, Digne-les-Bains

stops.name: Paris, the canon challenged
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1972; no month. The pin is the Paris publishing node and not a documented address
stops.campa: Three years after her death the physician Jeanne Denys publishes Alexandra David-Néel au Tibet: une supercherie dévoilée, arguing that she never entered Lhasa at all and that the photograph said to prove it was a montage. Jacques Brosse and other scholars reject the book as written in obvious bad faith. Both the charge and the rebuttal stand here, and neither photograph is re-verified. What stands outside the quarrel is the 1927 narrative: its streets, its dates, and the two months it accounts for hour by hour.
suggested_refs: Jeanne Denys, Alexandra David-Néel au Tibet: une supercherie dévoilée (1972)

stops.name: Varanasi, the ashes in the Ganges
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1973; no month recorded. Pin held byte-identical with the 1891 Varanasi stop to close the figure
stops.campa: In 1973 Marie-Madeleine Peyronnet carries two urns down to Benares, her employer's and Yongden's, and pours them into the Ganges together. He had waited eighteen years at Digne for her to be ready. The river is the one David-Néel came to in 1891, a woman of twenty-two spending an inheritance on a passage east, who sought out an ascetic on these ghats and went home to sing opera because the money had run out. She comes back to the same water eighty-two years later and stays.
suggested_refs: The immersion of the David-Néel and Yongden ashes at Varanasi, 1973
sources: Foster & Foster, The Secret Lives of Alexandra David-Néel

stops.name: Lhasa, the road walked again
stops.date_confidence: the sources conflict: English Wikipedia dates the expedition to 2006 and names the film Au Tibet interdit; French sources date the walk to 2002 and the film, Voyage au Tibet interdit, to 2005-2006. The earlier date is carried and the conflict is not resolved
stops.campa: Priscilla Telmon walks the route alone and on foot at twenty-seven: Vietnam, Yunnan, Tibet by way of Lhasa, then Sikkim and India, six months of it, and makes a film of the crossing. The sources disagree on whether the walk was in 2002 or 2006 and on what the film was called. Seventy-eight years after a Frenchwoman in soot and yak hair came up the Kyi valley with a monk and a revolver, another Frenchwoman does the same distance alone, with permits, and calls it a tribute.
suggested_refs: Priscilla Telmon, Au Tibet interdit / Voyage au Tibet interdit (2005-2006)
